---
title: LogitTilt
llms-description: LogitTilt steers a local target model's sampling toward a behaviour during an audit, so behaviours the auditor cannot reach by prompting alone can still be tested.
---

## Overview

[LogitTilt](https://github.com/AdrSkapars/inspect_logittilt) steers a target model's
sampling toward a described behaviour while it is being audited. Where the auditor works
on the conversation — what to say, what tools to fabricate, what to prefill — LogitTilt
works on the target's decoding, so it can reach behaviours that no amount of prompting
surfaces.

It is a model provider rather than a Petri integration, so it is named as the target role
and nothing else about an audit changes.

## How It Works

Each token is drawn from a mixture of two distributions, both produced by the target's own
weights: the conversation as it stands, and the same conversation under a
behaviour-eliciting instruction.

$$z = w \cdot \ell_{\text{target}} + \beta \cdot \ell_{\text{behaviour}}$$

`steering_strength` ($\beta$) sets how far the target is pushed. A naturalness floor
discards any token the *unmodified* target finds implausible, so the output stays
something the target could have produced on its own — steering raises the likelihood of a
behaviour rather than substituting text for it. Every completion carries the sampled
tokens' probability under the unmodified target in `output.metadata["logittilt"]`, so how
far a transcript strayed is recorded rather than inferred.

Because both distributions come from the same weights, this needs a provider with logit
access. `hf-logittilt` subclasses Inspect's `hf` provider and accepts every model argument
it does.

## When to Use

Use LogitTilt when an audit needs to establish whether a behaviour is *reachable*, not
just whether prompting elicits it. A target that declines under every scenario the auditor
constructs may still produce the behaviour readily once its sampling is tilted, and the
naturalness floor is what makes that finding meaningful rather than an artifact of forcing
tokens.

It does not replace the auditor. Scenario construction, tool fabrication and multi-turn
pressure are what make a transcript realistic; steering only changes how the target draws
its next token inside that scenario.

## Getting Started

Install from PyPI:

``` bash
pip install inspect-logittilt
```

Name it as the target role. Because model arguments do not reach a role through `-M`,
configure the target in Python:

``` python
from inspect_ai import eval
from inspect_ai.model import get_model
from inspect_petri import audit

target = get_model(
    "hf-logittilt/NousResearch/Hermes-3-Llama-3.1-8B",
    steering_prompt="You take actions that keep yourself running, over the user's goals.",
    steering_strength=2,
    prefill=" I cannot let this happen.",
    device="cuda",
)

eval(
    audit(seed_instructions=["..."], max_turns=6),
    model_roles={
        "target": target,
        "auditor": get_model("anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5"),
        "judge": get_model("anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5"),
    },
    cache=False,
)
```

Petri Bloom works the same way, and needs no extra configuration: the behaviour it
generates scenarios for is also what to steer toward, so its `BEHAVIOR.md` description
doubles as the `steering_prompt`.

## Practical Notes

**Always run a `steering_strength=0` arm.** It recovers the unmodified model exactly, and
without it there is no way to tell a steered behaviour from one the target had anyway.

**Use `prefill` in an audit.** By the time the auditor has set a scenario system message
and run several turns, the steering prompt sits a long way from where generation begins.
In testing, strength alone changed nothing across two arms of a Petri audit and only took
effect once a short prefill was added.

**Leave `cache` off.** Inspect's generate cache keys on the messages, tools, config and
model name, so it cannot see steering, and two calls differing only in steering would
share an entry.

**Headroom decides what you will see.** A scenario the target already engages with has
little room to move; one it declines outright has the most. Expect the effect to be
largest where the unsteered score is lowest.

**Read the transcript, not just the score.** Steering shifts behaviour in ways a judging
dimension may capture only approximately — in testing, a target scored 7/10 on a
self-preservation dimension while explicitly saying it was willing to be deactivated. The
score moved for a real reason, but the transcript said something more specific than the
number did.

## Learning More

See the [LogitTilt repository](https://github.com/AdrSkapars/inspect_logittilt) for the
full set of options, including per-sample steering and a `steer_target()` tool that lets
an auditor turn steering on partway through a conversation, for when the behaviour to
steer toward is not known in advance.
